title: Affective Factors & Classroom Climate

pts: Unit 8 applied Krashen's Affective Filter Hypothesis narrowly, to correction — this poster expands it to the whole classroom climate.
A high affective filter is argued to block comprehensible input from being processed for acquisition at all.
Climate-level anxiety can undo the value of even excellently designed lessons.

items: Recall a time you learned something while anxious, and a time you learned something while relaxed.
Compare: what did you remember? What did you attempt?
Discuss with a colleague: when does anxiety help (a little pressure before a test) and when does it block?
Identify one moment in your lessons where learners might feel high anxiety (reading aloud, being called on).
Plan one change to lower it.
In a training session, participants learn a few words of an unfamiliar language in a deliberately stressful way, then in a relaxed way, and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Reading aloud one by one → choral reading or pair reading.

blocks.x: The affective filter is a metaphor rather than a measurable mechanism, but it points to a real effect: anxious learners attempt less.

body: Purpose: to visualize the affective filter. Content: input shown as coloured dots flowing towards a learner’s head. A mesh screen sits in front of the head: dense and dark in the left panel (‘anxious’), with few dots getting through; open and light in the right panel (‘relaxed’), with many dots getting through. Style: simple, calm. Board version: two grids of different densities.

items: None needed; this is a reflection task.

pts: Foreign language anxiety is a specific form of anxiety tied to L2 performance, distinct from general nervousness.
It can affect confident, capable learners just as much as less able ones — competence and anxiety are not the same axis.
Recognising it as its own construct, not just 'shyness,' changes how a teacher responds to it.
points.who: Horwitz, Horwitz & Cope's Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale

items: Give learners a short, anonymous questionnaire with five statements (see model language).
Learners mark how true each statement is for them (1–5).
Summarize class results.
Share the results with the class: ‘Many of you feel nervous speaking in front of others. That’s normal.’
Plan changes based on the most common worries.
Repeat after a month to see if anything has changed.
Support: statements in the home language.

blocks.x: Questionnaire statements (written for this book, inspired by the themes in Horwitz et al. 1986):

lines: I feel nervous when the teacher asks me a question in English.
I worry that others will laugh at my English.
I know the answer but I don’t say it.
I feel more relaxed speaking English with a partner than with the whole class.

body: Purpose: to show how results can be displayed. Content: a horizontal bar chart of five statements with bars of different lengths showing how many learners agreed, without names. Style: clean, neutral colours. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Forms (free), anonymous, with a linear scale question.

blocks.x: Paper slips placed in a box.

pts: Willingness to communicate is a learner's momentary readiness to speak, shaped heavily by the immediate context.
The same learner may be highly willing to speak in a small pair task and completely unwilling in a whole-class one.
Task and grouping design (Unit 7, Unit 15) directly influence this moment-to-moment willingness.
points.who: Peter MacIntyre's Willingness to Communicate model

items: Start with private thinking time (30 seconds).
Learners tell a partner their answer.
Pairs join another pair and share.
Invite volunteers to share with the class, or share ‘your partner’s idea’.
Notice how many more learners speak than in whole-class questioning.
Use ‘inside–outside circles’ for repeated, short conversations with new partners.
Support: sentence frames.
Stretch: ask follow-up questions.

blocks.x: Sharing a partner’s idea is less risky than sharing one’s own:

lines: Ravi thinks the best festival is Ugadi because of the food.

blocks.x: Willingness to communicate depends on the situation: the same learner may speak freely in a pair and stay silent in front of the class (MacIntyre et al. 1998).

body: Purpose: to show a gradual widening of audience. Content: four nested circles: innermost ‘think alone’, then ‘tell a partner’, then ‘tell a group of four’, then outermost ‘tell the class’. A small figure moves outwards through them. Style: clean, concentric. Board version: four circles.

items: Padlet (free plan). Learners post answers anonymously before any spoken sharing.

blocks.x: Written answers on slips, read aloud by the teacher without names.

pts: Rapport is built through small, consistent behaviours — learning names, showing genuine interest — more than grand gestures.
Rapport built early in a course pays off across every later lesson's willingness to take communicative risks.
This is a deliberately built skill, not a fixed personality trait some teachers simply have and others don't.

v: Class list with photos or seating plan

items: Learn every learner’s name within two weeks, using a seating plan.
Pronounce names correctly; ask learners to teach you if unsure.
Greet learners at the door when possible.
Remember and ask about one thing each learner mentioned (a match, a sibling’s wedding).
Keep promises made to the class.
Learners make name cards with a drawing of something they like.
Not applicable (teacher behaviour).

blocks.x: Small, consistent behaviours that build rapport:

lines: Good morning, Fatima. How was the cricket match?
Sorry, did I say your name correctly? Tell me again.
I said I’d bring the story today, and here it is.

body: Purpose: to show rapport-building behaviours. Content: a teacher at a classroom door greeting learners by name, with small speech bubbles showing names and short personal questions. Style: warm, inclusive illustration. Board version: not applicable.

items: A seating plan in a notes app with learners’ names.

blocks.x: A paper seating plan in the register.

pts: Used well, humour lowers the stakes of language production and increases risk-taking without undermining seriousness.
Playful framing of a task can achieve the same practice goal as a serious one, with lower affective cost.
This is compatible with, not opposed to, rigorous language work — the two aren't in tension.

items: Give pairs cards with nouns, verbs and places.
Pairs build the silliest grammatically correct sentence they can (The elephant is dancing on the bus.).
Pairs read sentences aloud; the class votes for the funniest.
Everyone repeats the winning sentence.
Return to the lesson’s serious task, now with lighter energy.
Use target grammar: Yesterday my teacher went to the moon and ate…
Support: fewer word cards.
Stretch: sentences must use a given structure.

lines: Laugh at situations, words and the teacher’s own mistakes, never at a learner.
I just said ‘I goed’. Oops! What should I say?

body: Purpose: to show inclusive humour. Content: a class laughing with the teacher at a silly sentence on the board (The elephant is dancing on the bus), with a drawing of an elephant on a bus. No learner is singled out. Style: cheerful. Board version: the sentence and a quick drawing.

items: Wordwall (free basic version) random-word spinner for sentence building.

body: When you make a mistake in English, correct it openly and with good humour. Learners who see their teacher handle mistakes calmly learn that mistakes are a normal part of using a language.

pts: A classroom where mistakes are visibly treated as normal produces more output than one where they're implicitly punished.
This connects directly to Unit 8's correction hierarchy — how correction is delivered shapes perceived safety.
Safety is established through consistent teacher response over time, not a single announced rule.

items: Ask learners how they feel when they make a mistake in English.
Together, write class agreements about mistakes (see model language).
Learners sign or draw on the chart.
Display it and refer to it when needed.
Celebrate ‘useful mistakes’ that helped the class learn.
A ‘mistake of the week’ award for the most useful mistake (with permission, anonymous if preferred).
Support: agreements in the home language alongside English.

lines: Mistakes help us learn. We never laugh at someone’s English. We help each other. It’s OK to say ‘I don’t know yet’.

body: Purpose: a wall poster. Content: a chart with four short agreements in large letters, decorated with learners’ handprints or signatures around the border. Style: warm, handmade. Board version: not applicable.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printed version.

pts: A learner's belief in their own capability predicts persistence with a task more reliably than their actual ability does.
Specific, achievable success experiences build self-efficacy more effectively than general encouragement.
This connects to Unit 8's guidance on specific, process-focused praise over generic praise.

items: Break a difficult goal into small, achievable steps.
Ensure each learner experiences success on a step early.
Give specific feedback on what they did well (Unit 8).
Learners record successes in a ‘can-do’ log.
Before a hard task, remind learners of earlier successes.
Peer ‘success stories’: learners tell a partner one thing they can now do.
Support: smaller steps.
Stretch: larger steps with more independence.

blocks.x: Steps towards giving a one-minute talk:

lines: 1. Say three sentences to a partner. 2. Say five sentences with notes. 3. Say one minute with notes. 4. Say one minute to a group. 5. Say one minute to the class.

blocks.x: Self-efficacy, a person’s belief in their ability to succeed at a task, grows most from actual success experiences (Bandura 1997).

body: Purpose: to show self-efficacy built through small successes. Content: a staircase of five steps from ‘three sentences to a partner’ to ‘one minute to the class’, with a small figure climbing and a star on each step reached. Style: encouraging, clean. Board version: five steps.

items: Google Sheets (free) for learners with access to record successes.

blocks.x: A can-do log page in the notebook.

pts: Teacher enthusiasm and stress are both contagious within a classroom.
Managing one's own affective state is, practically, part of managing the room's climate as a whole.
This is not about performing constant positivity, but about noticing and managing your own state's effect on the room.

items: Before a lesson, notice your own state: tired, anxious, energized, irritated.
Choose one small action to bring yourself to a steady state (a breath, a smile at the door, a glass of water).
After the lesson, note how your mood seemed to affect the class.
Over two weeks, look for patterns.
Plan routines that support your own wellbeing on difficult days.
Share strategies with colleagues.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Monday: I was rushed and irritable. The class was noisy and I raised my voice. Tuesday: I arrived five minutes early and greeted them at the door. Calmer lesson.

blocks.x: Research suggests that teachers’ enjoyment and enthusiasm can be transmitted to learners (Frenzel et al. 2009).

body: Purpose: to show emotional contagion. Content: two classroom scenes. In the first, a storm cloud above the teacher and small clouds above learners. In the second, sunshine above the teacher and small suns above learners. Style: gentle, not judgemental. Board version: not applicable.

items: Any notes app for a brief daily log.

blocks.x: A small notebook kept in the bag.

body: For one week, stand at the door and greet each learner by name as they enter. At the end of the week, compare the first ten minutes of lessons with the week before. Many teachers notice a calmer, more willing start.

dek: Unit 22 of 100: anxiety, willingness to communicate and rapport shape whether well-designed teaching actually reaches the learner in front of you.

aims.x: This unit examines the feelings that surround language learning: anxiety, confidence, willingness to speak, and the relationship between teacher and learners. It treats classroom climate as a condition for learning rather than an optional extra.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the affective filter and its limits as a model;
recognize foreign language anxiety and respond to it;
design tasks that raise learners’ willingness to communicate;
build rapport through small, consistent behaviours;
use humour and play to lower stakes without lowering standards;
create a climate where mistakes are normal;
build learners’ self-efficacy through specific success;
notice and manage your own emotional state in the classroom.

why: Why this matters. The best-planned task fails if the learner is too anxious to attempt it. Climate isn't a soft add-on to methodology — it's a condition for methodology to work at all.

background.x: Every experienced teacher has seen it: a learner who knows the answer but will not say it, a class that freezes when asked to speak, a confident child who becomes silent in a new school. Language learning is unusually exposed to feeling. Speaking a new language means sounding less intelligent, less funny and less oneself than one really is, often in front of peers. It is not surprising that emotions shape how much learners attempt, and therefore how much they learn.

Stephen Krashen (1982) proposed the affective filter as a way of describing this: when anxiety is high or motivation low, input may not be processed for acquisition, however good it is. The metaphor has been criticized as too vague to test, but it captured something teachers recognized immediately. Since then, researchers have studied specific emotions in more detail. Elaine Horwitz and colleagues (1986) identified foreign language classroom anxiety as a distinct phenomenon. Peter MacIntyre and colleagues (1998) developed the idea of willingness to communicate, which varies from moment to moment depending on the situation. More recently, Jean-Marc Dewaele and MacIntyre (2014) have shown that enjoyment matters as much as anxiety: a classroom can be both challenging and enjoyable, and enjoyment supports learning.

These ideas matter in Indian classrooms in particular ways. English often carries social prestige, and learners may feel that their English is being judged as a sign of their background or intelligence. Some learners have been laughed at for their pronunciation or corrected harshly in the past. A teacher who understands this can make the English classroom a place where learners are willing to try.

items: Anxiety survey trend. Compare class anxiety results at the start and end of a term.
Participation spread. Count how many learners speak in a lesson before and after introducing low-stakes routines.
Can-do logs. Review success records to see progress towards targets.
Learner feedback. A short anonymous question each term: ‘Do you feel safe making mistakes in English class?’
Which learners in your class are quiet? Is it because they don’t know, or because they are anxious?
When did a learner last laugh at another’s English in your class? How did you respond?
What do you do to learn and use learners’ names?
How does your mood on a given day show up in your teaching?
What would your learners say makes the English classroom feel safe?

terms.def: Emotional and attitudinal influences on learning, such as anxiety, motivation, self-confidence and attitudes to the language, which can make learners more or less willing to take part and take risks.
Krashen’s (1982) metaphor for emotional states such as anxiety or low confidence that block input from being acquired; a relaxed, supportive classroom is said to lower the filter.
The emotional and social atmosphere of a classroom, including how safe learners feel to speak, take risks and make mistakes.
The tendency for emotions to spread from one person to others in a group. In class, a teacher’s enthusiasm or anxiety can quickly shape the mood and willingness to speak of the whole room.

The positive emotion learners feel when a class is both challenging and satisfying. Research on foreign language enjoyment suggests it matters as much as anxiety and supports learning (Dewaele and MacIntyre 2014).
The worry and nervousness specific to using or learning a foreign language, such as fear of speaking in front of others or of negative evaluation (Horwitz, Horwitz and Cope 1986).

A positive, trusting relationship between teacher and learners, built through respect, warmth, fairness and genuine interest in learners, which encourages participation and willingness to take risks in English.

A person’s belief in their ability to succeed at a particular task (Bandura 1977). Learners with higher self-efficacy in English persist longer and take more risks; achievable tasks and specific praise help to build it.

A learner’s readiness to enter into communication in a second language at a particular time with particular people (MacIntyre et al. 1998). It is influenced by confidence, anxiety and the classroom climate.
